7: 
8: # Reusing Reducer Logic
9: 
10: As an application grows, common patterns in reducer logic will start to emerge. You may find several parts of your reducer logic doing the same kinds of work for different types of data, and want to reduce duplication by reusing the same common logic for each data type. Or, you may want to have multiple "instances" of a certain type of data being handled in the store. However, the global structure of a Redux store comes with some trade-offs: it makes it easy to track the overall state of an application, but can also make it harder to "target" actions that need to update a specific piece of state, particularly if you are using `combineReducers`.
11: 
12: As an example, let's say that we want to track multiple counters in our application, named A, B, and C. We define our initial `counter` reducer, and we use `combineReducers` to set up our state:
13: 
14: ```js
15: function counter(state = 0, action) {
16:   switch (action.type) {
17:     case 'INCREMENT':
18:       return state + 1
19:     case 'DECREMENT':
20:       return state - 1
21:     default:
22:       return state
23:   }
24: }
25: 
26: const rootReducer = combineReducers({
27:   counterA: counter,
28:   counterB: counter,
29:   counterC: counter
30: })
31: ```
32: 
33: Unfortunately, this setup has a problem. Because `combineReducers` will call each slice reducer with the same action, dispatching `{type : 'INCREMENT'}` will actually cause _all three_ counter values to be incremented, not just one of them. We need some way to wrap the `counter` logic so that we can ensure that only the counter we care about is updated.
34: 
35: ## Customizing Behavior with Higher-Order Reducers
36: 
37: As defined in [Splitting Reducer Logic](SplittingReducerLogic.md), a _higher-order reducer_ is a function that takes a reducer function as an argument, and/or returns a new reducer function as a result. It can also be viewed as a "reducer factory". `combineReducers` is one example of a higher-order reducer. We can use this pattern to create specialized versions of our own reducer functions, with each version only responding to specific actions.
38: 
39: The two most common ways to specialize a reducer are to generate new action constants with a given prefix or suffix, or to attach additional info inside the action object. Here's what those might look like:
40: 
41: ```js
42: function createCounterWithNamedType(counterName = '') {
43:   return function counter(state = 0, action) {
44:     switch (action.type) {
45:       case `INCREMENT_${counterName}`:
46:         return state + 1
47:       case `DECREMENT_${counterName}`:
48:         return state - 1
49:       default:
50:         return state
51:     }
52:   }
53: }
54: 
55: function createCounterWithNameData(counterName = '') {
56:   return function counter(state = 0, action) {
57:     const { name } = action
58:     if (name !== counterName) return state
59: 
60:     switch (action.type) {
61:       case `INCREMENT`:
62:         return state + 1
63:       case `DECREMENT`:
64:         return state - 1
65:       default:
66:         return state
67:     }
68:   }
69: }
70: ```
71: 
72: We should now be able to use either of these to generate our specialized counter reducers, and then dispatch actions that will affect the portion of the state that we care about:
73: 
74: ```js
75: const rootReducer = combineReducers({
76:   counterA: createCounterWithNamedType('A'),
77:   counterB: createCounterWithNamedType('B'),
78:   counterC: createCounterWithNamedType('C')
79: })
80: 
81: store.dispatch({ type: 'INCREMENT_B' })
82: console.log(store.getState())
83: // {counterA : 0, counterB : 1, counterC : 0}
84: ```
85: 
86: We could also vary the approach somewhat, and create a more generic higher-order reducer that accepts both a given reducer function and a name or identifier:
87: 
88: ```js
89: function counter(state = 0, action) {
90:   switch (action.type) {
91:     case 'INCREMENT':
92:       return state + 1
93:     case 'DECREMENT':
94:       return state - 1
95:     default:
96:       return state
97:   }
98: }
99: 
100: function createNamedWrapperReducer(reducerFunction, reducerName) {
101:   return (state, action) => {
102:     const { name } = action
103:     const isInitializationCall = state === undefined
104:     if (name !== reducerName && !isInitializationCall) return state
105: 
106:     return reducerFunction(state, action)
107:   }
108: }
109: 
110: const rootReducer = combineReducers({
111:   counterA: createNamedWrapperReducer(counter, 'A'),
112:   counterB: createNamedWrapperReducer(counter, 'B'),
113:   counterC: createNamedWrapperReducer(counter, 'C')
114: })
115: ```
116: 
117: You could even go as far as to make a generic filtering higher-order reducer:
118: 
119: ```js
120: function createFilteredReducer(reducerFunction, reducerPredicate) {
121:     return (state, action) => {
122:         const isInitializationCall = state === undefined;
123:         const shouldRunWrappedReducer = reducerPredicate(action) || isInitializationCall;
124:         return shouldRunWrappedReducer ? reducerFunction(state, action) : state;
125:     }
126: }
127: 
128: const rootReducer = combineReducers({
129:     // check for suffixed strings
130:     counterA : createFilteredReducer(counter, action => action.type.endsWith('_A')),
131:     // check for extra data in the action
132:     counterB : createFilteredReducer(counter, action => action.name === 'B'),
133:     // respond to all 'INCREMENT' actions, but never 'DECREMENT'
134:     counterC : createFilteredReducer(counter, action => action.type === 'INCREMENT')
135: };
136: ```
137: 
138: These basic patterns allow you to do things like having multiple instances of a smart connected component within the UI, or reuse common logic for generic capabilities such as pagination or sorting.
139: 
140: In addition to generating reducers this way, you might also want to generate action creators using the same approach, and could generate them both at the same time with helper functions. See [Action/Reducer Generators](https://github.com/markerikson/redux-ecosystem-links/blob/master/action-reducer-generators.md) and [Reducers](https://github.com/markerikson/redux-ecosystem-links/blob/master/reducers.md) libraries for action/reducer utilities.

7: 
8: # Splitting Up Reducer Logic
9: 
10: For any meaningful application, putting _all_ your update logic into a single reducer function is quickly going to become unmaintainable. While there's no single rule for how long a function should be, it's generally agreed that functions should be relatively short and ideally only do one specific thing. Because of this, it's good programming practice to take pieces of code that are very long or do many different things, and break them into smaller pieces that are easier to understand.
11: 
12: Since a Redux reducer is _just_ a function, the same concept applies. You can split some of your reducer logic out into another function, and call that new function from the parent function.
13: 
14: These new functions would typically fall into one of three categories:
15: 
16: 1. Small utility functions containing some reusable chunk of logic that is needed in multiple places (which may or may not be actually related to the specific business logic)
17: 2. Functions for handling a specific update case, which often need parameters other than the typical `(state, action)` pair
18: 3. Functions which handle _all_ updates for a given slice of state. These functions do generally have the typical `(state, action)` parameter signature
19: 
20: For clarity, these terms will be used to distinguish between different types of functions and different use cases:
21: 
22: - **_reducer_**: any function with the signature `(state, action) -> newState` (ie, any function that _could_ be used as an argument to `Array.prototype.reduce`)
23: - **_root reducer_**: the reducer function that is actually passed as the first argument to `createStore`. This is the only part of the reducer logic that _must_ have the `(state, action) -> newState` signature.
24: - **_slice reducer_**: a reducer that is being used to handle updates to one specific slice of the state tree, usually done by passing it to `combineReducers`
25: - **_case function_**: a function that is being used to handle the update logic for a specific action. This may actually be a reducer function, or it may require other parameters to do its work properly.
26: - **_higher-order reducer_**: a function that takes a reducer function as an argument, and/or returns a new reducer function as a result (such as `combineReducers`, or `redux-undo`)
27: 
28: The term "_sub-reducer_" has also been used in various discussions to mean any function that is not the root reducer, although the term is not very precise. Some people may also refer to some functions as "_business logic_" (functions that relate to application-specific behavior) or "_utility functions_" (generic functions that are not application-specific).
29: 
30: Breaking down a complex process into smaller, more understandable parts is usually described with the term **_[functional decomposition](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/947874/what-is-functional-decomposition)_**. This term and concept can be applied generically to any code. However, in Redux it is _very_ common to structure reducer logic using approach #3, where update logic is delegated to other functions based on slice of state. Redux refers to this concept as **_reducer composition_**, and it is by far the most widely-used approach to structuring reducer logic. In fact, it's so common that Redux includes a utility function called [`combineReducers()`](../../api/combineReducers.md), which specifically abstracts the process of delegating work to other reducer functions based on slices of state. However, it's important to note that it is not the _only_ pattern that can be used. In fact, it's entirely possible to use all three approaches for splitting up logic into functions, and usually a good idea as well. The [Refactoring Reducers](./RefactoringReducersExample.md) section shows some examples of this in action.

(End of file - total 30 lines)
</content>

142: ## Collection / Item Reducer Pattern
143: 
144: While higher-order reducers are most commonly used to specialize a single reducer for a specific piece of state, they can also be used to manage _collections_ of similar state slices. The "collection / item reducer pattern" allows you to reuse the same reducer logic across multiple instances of state, updating only the specific item that an action targets based on an additional parameter (such as an index or a name) included in the action object.
145: 
146: This can be particularly useful if you need to manage many instances of the same type of data and the number of instances is not known ahead of time, since it is difficult (or impossible) to set up a fixed set of slice reducers in a `combineReducers` call. In general, though, this pattern should only be used if you are confident that the range of possible collection sizes is small, or if the data is not going to be nested as deeply.
147: 
148: Here's a typical set up, with a basic `counter` reducer that handles `INCREMENT` and `DECREMENT` actions:
149: 
150: ```js
151: function counter(state = 0, action) {
152:   switch (action.type) {
153:     case 'INCREMENT':
154:       return state + 1
155:     case 'DECREMENT':
156:       return state - 1
157:     default:
158:       return state
159:   }
160: }
161: ```
162: 
163: We can use this reducer with an array, where each item in the collection is updated by targeting its `position` in the array. Every time an action is dispatched, we use the `index` property included in the action to figure out which item in the array should be updated, and then use array spread and slicing to produce a new array with the updated item in place:
164: 
165: ```js
166: function counters(state = [], action) {
167:   const { index } = action
168: 
169:   if (index === undefined) {
170:     return state
171:   }
172: 
173:   switch (action.type) {
174:     case 'INCREMENT':
175:       return [
176:         ...state.slice(0, index),
177:         ...[(state[index] || 0) + 1],
178:         ...state.slice(index + 1)
179:       ]
180:     case 'DECREMENT':
181:       return [
182:         ...state.slice(0, index),
183:         ...[(state[index] || 0) - 1],
184:         ...state.slice(index + 1)
185:       ]
186:     default:
187:       return state
188:   }
189: }
190: ```
191: 
192: For an object/map-based collection, we can instead include a `name` property in the action to identify which piece of state we want to update. The reducer for the collection can then use object spread and computed property names to generate a new object with only the specified key updated, leaving all other entries untouched:
193: 
194: ```js
195: const initialState = {
196:   A: 0,
197:   B: 0,
198:   C: 0
199: }
200: 
201: function counters(state = initialState, action) {
202:   const { key } = action
203: 
204:   if (key === undefined) {
205:     return state
206:   }
207: 
208:   switch (action.type) {
209:     case 'INCREMENT':
210:       return {
211:         ...state,
212:         [key]: state[key] + 1
213:       }
214:     case 'DECREMENT':
215:       return {
216:         ...state,
217:         [key]: state[key] - 1
218:       }
219:     default:
220:       return state
221:   }
222: }
223: ```
224: 
225: Note that this approach is effectively equivalent to using higher-order reducers like `createCounterWithNameData` from above to generate a slice reducer for each item in the collection, but without requiring a fixed set of slice reducers to be set up in advance via `combineReducers`. Instead, a single reducer manages the entire collection, and the "which item to update" decision is made purely from the information included in each action.

+## Collection / Item Reducer Pattern
+
+While higher-order reducers are most commonly used to specialize a single reducer for a specific piece of state, they can also be used to manage _collections_ of similar state slices. The "collection / item reducer pattern" allows you to reuse the same reducer logic across multiple instances of state, updating only the specific item that an action targets based on an additional parameter (such as an index or a name) included in the action object.
+
+This can be particularly useful if you need to manage many instances of the same type of data and the number of instances is not known ahead of time, since it is difficult (or impossible) to set up a fixed set of slice reducers in a `combineReducers` call. In general, though, this pattern should only be used if you are confident that the range of possible collection sizes is small, or if the data is not going to be nested as deeply.
+
+Here's a typical set up, with a basic `counter` reducer that handles `INCREMENT` and `DECREMENT` actions:
+
+```js
+function counter(state = 0, action) {
+  switch (action.type) {
+    case 'INCREMENT':
+      return state + 1
+    case 'DECREMENT':
+      return state - 1
+    default:
+      return state
+  }
+}
+```
+
+We can use this reducer with an array, where each item in the collection is updated by targeting its `position` in the array. Every time an action is dispatched, we use the `index` property included in the action to figure out which item in the array should be updated, and then use array spread and slicing to produce a new array with the updated item in place:
+
+```js
+function counters(state = [], action) {
+  const { index } = action
+
+  if (index === undefined) {
+    return state
+  }

7: 
8: # Immutable Update Patterns
9: 
10: The articles listed in [Prerequisite Concepts#Immutable Data Management](PrerequisiteConcepts.md#immutable-data-management) give a number of good examples for how to perform basic update operations immutably, such as updating a field in an object or adding an item to the end of an array. However, reducers will often need to use those basic operations in combination to perform more complicated tasks. Here are some examples for some of the more common tasks you might have to implement.
11: 
12: ## Updating Nested Objects
13: 
14: The key to updating nested data is **that _every_ level of nesting must be copied and updated appropriately**. This is often a difficult concept for those learning Redux, and there are some specific problems that frequently occur when trying to update nested objects. These lead to accidental direct mutation, and should be avoided.
15: 
16: ##### Common Mistake #1: New variables that point to the same objects
17: 
18: Defining a new variable does _not_ create a new actual object - it only creates another reference to the same object. An example of this error would be:
19: 
20: ```js
21: function updateNestedState(state, action) {
22:   let nestedState = state.nestedState
23:   // ERROR: this directly modifies the existing object reference - don't do this!
24:   nestedState.nestedField = action.data
25: 
26:   return {
27:     ...state,
28:     nestedState
29:   }
30: }
31: ```
32: 
33: This function does correctly return a shallow copy of the top-level state object, but because the `nestedState` variable was still pointing at the existing object, the state was directly mutated.
34: 
35: ##### Common Mistake #2: Only making a shallow copy of one level
36: 
37: Another common version of this error looks like this:
38: 
39: ```js
40: function updateNestedState(state, action) {
41:   // Problem: this only does a shallow copy!
42:   let newState = { ...state }
43: 
44:   // ERROR: nestedState is still the same object!
45:   newState.nestedState.nestedField = action.data
46: 
47:   return newState
48: }
49: ```
50: 
51: Doing a shallow copy of the top level is _not_ sufficient - the `nestedState` object should be copied as well.
52: 
53: ##### Correct Approach: Copying All Levels of Nested Data
54: 
55: Unfortunately, the process of correctly applying immutable updates to deeply nested state can easily become verbose and hard to read. Here's what an example of updating `state.first.second[someId].fourth` might look like:
56: 
57: ```js
58: function updateVeryNestedField(state, action) {
59:   return {
60:     ...state,
61:     first: {
62:       ...state.first,
63:       second: {
64:         ...state.first.second,
65:         [action.someId]: {
66:           ...state.first.second[action.someId],
67:           fourth: action.someValue
68:         }
69:       }
70:     }
71:   }
72: }
73: ```
74: 
75: Obviously, each layer of nesting makes this harder to read, and gives more chances to make mistakes. This is one of several reasons why you are encouraged to keep your state flattened, and compose reducers as much as possible.
76: 
77: ## Inserting and Removing Items in Arrays
78: 
79: Normally, a Javascript array's contents are modified using mutative functions like `push`, `unshift`, and `splice`. Since we don't want to mutate state directly in reducers, those should normally be avoided. Because of that, you might see "insert" or "remove" behavior written like this:
80: 
81: ```js
82: function insertItem(array, action) {
83:   return [
84:     ...array.slice(0, action.index),
85:     action.item,
86:     ...array.slice(action.index)
87:   ]
88: }
89: 
90: function removeItem(array, action) {
91:   return [...array.slice(0, action.index), ...array.slice(action.index + 1)]
92: }
93: ```
94: 
95: However, remember that the key is that the _original in-memory reference_ is not modified. **As long as we make a copy first, we can safely mutate the copy**. Note that this is true for both arrays and objects, but nested values still must be updated using the same rules.
96: 
97: This means that we could also write the insert and remove functions like this:
98: 
99: ```js
100: function insertItem(array, action) {
101:   let newArray = array.slice()
102:   newArray.splice(action.index, 0, action.item)
103:   return newArray
104: }
105: 
106: function removeItem(array, action) {
107:   let newArray = array.slice()
108:   newArray.splice(action.index, 1)
109:   return newArray
110: }
111: ```
112: 
113: The remove function could also be implemented as:
114: 
115: ```js
116: function removeItem(array, action) {
117:   return array.filter((item, index) => index !== action.index)
118: }
119: ```
120: 
121: ## Updating an Item in an Array
122: 
123: Updating one item in an array can be accomplished by using `Array.map`, returning a new value for the item we want to update, and returning the existing values for all other items:
124: 
125: ```js
126: function updateObjectInArray(array, action) {
127:   return array.map((item, index) => {
128:     if (index !== action.index) {
129:       // This isn't the item we care about - keep it as-is
130:       return item
131:     }
132: 
133:     // Otherwise, this is the one we want - return an updated value
134:     return {
135:       ...item,
136:       ...action.item
137:     }
138:   })
139: }
140: ```
141: 
142: ## Immutable Update Utility Libraries
143: 
144: Because writing immutable update code can become tedious, there are a number of utility libraries that try to abstract out the process. These libraries vary in APIs and usage, but all try to provide a shorter and more succinct way of writing these updates. For example, [Immer](https://github.com/mweststrate/immer) makes immutable updates a simple function and plain JavaScript objects:
145: 
146: ```js
147: var usersState = [{ name: 'John Doe', address: { city: 'London' } }]
148: var newState = immer.produce(usersState, draftState => {
149:   draftState[0].name = 'Jon Doe'
150:   draftState[0].address.city = 'Paris'
151:   //nested update similar to mutable way
152: })
153: ```
154: 
155: Some, like [dot-prop-immutable](https://github.com/debitoor/dot-prop-immutable), take string paths for commands:
156: 
157: ```js
158: state = dotProp.set(state, `todos.${index}.complete`, true)
159: ```
160: 
161: Others, like [immutability-helper](https://github.com/kolodny/immutability-helper) (a fork of the now-deprecated React Immutability Helpers addon), use nested values and helper functions:
162: 
163: ```js
164: var collection = [1, 2, { a: [12, 17, 15] }]
165: var newCollection = update(collection, {
166:   2: { a: { $splice: [[1, 1, 13, 14]] } }
167: })
168: ```
169: 
170: They can provide a useful alternative to writing manual immutable update logic.
171: 
172: A list of many immutable update utilities can be found in the [Immutable Data#Immutable Update Utilities](https://github.com/markerikson/redux-ecosystem-links/blob/master/immutable-data.md#immutable-update-utilities) section of the [Redux Addons Catalog](https://github.com/markerikson/redux-ecosystem-links).
173: 
174: ## Simplifying Immutable Updates with Redux Starter Kit
175: 
176: Our [Redux Starter Kit](https://redux-starter-kit.js.org/) package includes a [`createReducer` utility](https://redux-starter-kit.js.org/api/createReducer) that uses Immer internally.
177: Because of this, you can write reducers that appear to "mutate" state, but the updates are actually applied immutably.
178: 
179: This allows immutable update logic to be written in a much simpler way. Here's what the [nested data example](#correct-approach-copying-all-levels-of-nested-data)
180: might look like using `createReducer`:
181: 
182: ```js
183: import { createReducer } from 'redux-starter-kit'
184: 
185: const initialState = {
186:   first: {
187:     second: {
188:       id1: { fourth: 'a' },
189:       id2: { fourth: 'b' }
190:     }
191:   }
192: }
193: 
194: const reducer = createReducer(initialState, {
195:   UPDATE_ITEM: (state, action) => {
196:     state.first.second[action.someId].fourth = action.someValue
197:   }
198: })
199: ```
200: 
201: This is clearly _much_ shorter and easier to read. However, **this _only_ works correctly if you are using the "magic"
202: `createReducer` function from Redux Starter Kit** that wraps this reducer in Immer's [`produce` function](https://github.com/mweststrate/immer#api).  
203: **If this reducer is used without Immer, it will actually mutate the state!**. It's also not obvious just by
204: looking at the code that this function is actually safe and updates the state immutably. Please make sure you understand
205: the concepts of immutable updates fully. If you do use this, it may help to add some comments to your code that explain
206: your reducers are using Redux Starter Kit and Immer.

(End of file - total 206 lines)

The current `Middleware` type definition in `src/types/middleware.ts` uses `any` for the action parameter in the returned dispatch function, which disables type checking for middleware. This leads to loss of type safety when working with middleware that dispatches actions.

    The goal is to improve the `Middleware` type so that the action type flows through correctly, enabling TypeScript to validate action types in middleware implementations. Specifically, the `next` parameter and the returned dispatch function should use the dispatch type's action type rather than relying on `any` or a fixed `AnyAction` type.

    Please update the `Middleware` interface to:
    - Remove the import of `AnyAction` (no longer needed)
    - Change the `next` parameter from `Dispatch<AnyAction>` to the generic dispatch type `D`
    - Derive the action type for the returned function from the dispatch type's action type using conditional type inference

    This change should be backward-compatible for existing middleware that don't specify type parameters, while providing better type safety for those that do.

## Environment Setup
Check the following repo files for setup and testing instructions:
    - `package.json` (root) — for npm scripts, dependencies, and test commands

    - `test/typescript/tsconfig.json` — for TypeScript test configuration
    - `test/typescript/middleware.ts` — for existing middleware type tests
    - `.eslintrc.js` — for linting rules

## Implementation Plan

    - Remove the `AnyAction` import from `./actions`
    - Update the return type of the middleware: change the `next` parameter from `Dispatch<AnyAction>` to the generic `D` type parameter
    - Use conditional type inference on the `next` parameter: `(action: D extends Dispatch<infer A> ? A : never) => any` to derive the action type from the dispatch type
    - Verify the change works with existing TypeScript tests in `test/typescript/middleware.ts` by running the test suite

7: 
8: # Usage with TypeScript
9: 
10: **TypeScript** is a typed superset of JavaScript. It has become popular recently in applications due to the benefits it can bring. If you are new to TypeScript it is highly recommended to become familiar with it first before proceeding. You can check out its documentation [here.](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/typescript-in-5-minutes.html)
11: 
12: TypeScript has the potential to bring the following benefits to a Redux application:
13: 
14: 1. Type safety for reducers, state and action creators
15: 2. Easy refactoring of typed code
16: 3. A superior developer experience in a team environment
17: 
18: ## A Practical Example
19: 
20: We will be going through a simplistic chat application to demonstrate a possible approach to include static typing. This chat application will have two reducers. The _chat reducer_ will focus on storing the chat history and the _system reducer_ will focus on storing session information.
21: 
22: The full source code is available on [codesandbox here](https://codesandbox.io/s/w02m7jm3q7). Note that by going through this example yourself you will experience some of the benefits of using TypeScript.
23: 
24: ## Type Checking State
25: 
26: Adding types to each slice of state is a good place to start since it does not rely on other types. In this example we start by describing the chat reducer's slice of state:
27: 
28: ```ts
29: // src/store/chat/types.ts
30: 
31: export interface Message {
32:   user: string
33:   message: string
34:   timestamp: number
35: }
36: 
37: export interface ChatState {
38:   messages: Message[]
39: }
40: ```
41: 
42: And then do the same for the system reducer's slice of state:
43: 
44: ```ts
45: // src/store/system/types.ts
46: 
47: export interface SystemState {
48:   loggedIn: boolean
49:   session: string
50:   userName: string
51: }
52: ```
53: 
54: Note that we are exporting these interfaces to reuse them later in reducers and action creators.
55: 
56: ## Type Checking Actions & Action Creators
57: 
58: We will be using string literals and using `typeof` to declare our action constants and infer types. Note that we are making a tradeoff here when we declare our types in a separate file. In exchange for separating our types into a separate file, we get to keep our other files more focused on their purpose. While this tradeoff can improve the maintainability of the codebase, it is perfectly fine to organize your project however you see fit.
59: 
60: Chat Action Constants & Shape:
61: 
62: ```ts
63: // src/store/chat/types.ts
64: export const SEND_MESSAGE = 'SEND_MESSAGE'
65: export const DELETE_MESSAGE = 'DELETE_MESSAGE'
66: 
67: interface SendMessageAction {
68:   type: typeof SEND_MESSAGE
69:   payload: Message
70: }
71: 
72: interface DeleteMessageAction {
73:   type: typeof DELETE_MESSAGE
74:   meta: {
75:     timestamp: number
76:   }
77: }
78: 
79: export type ChatActionTypes = SendMessageAction | DeleteMessageAction
80: ```
81: 
82: Note that we are using TypeScript's Union Type here to express all possible actions.
83: 
84: With these types declared we can now also type check chat's action creators. In this case we are taking advantage of TypeScript's inference:
85: 
86: ```ts
87: // src/store/chat/actions.ts
88: 
89: import { Message, SEND_MESSAGE, DELETE_MESSAGE, ChatActionTypes } from './types'
90: 
91: // TypeScript infers that this function is returning SendMessageAction
92: export function sendMessage(newMessage: Message): ChatActionTypes {
93:   return {
94:     type: SEND_MESSAGE,
95:     payload: newMessage
96:   }
97: }
98: 
99: // TypeScript infers that this function is returning DeleteMessageAction
100: export function deleteMessage(timestamp: number): ChatActionTypes {
101:   return {
102:     type: DELETE_MESSAGE,
103:     meta: {
104:       timestamp
105:     }
106:   }
107: }
108: ```
109: 
110: System Action Constants & Shape:
111: 
112: ```ts
113: // src/store/system/types.ts
114: export const UPDATE_SESSION = 'UPDATE_SESSION'
115: 
116: interface UpdateSessionAction {
117:   type: typeof UPDATE_SESSION
118:   payload: SystemState
119: }
120: 
121: export type SystemActionTypes = UpdateSessionAction
122: ```
123: 
124: With these types we can now also type check system's action creators:
125: 
126: ```ts
127: // src/store/system/actions.ts
128: 
129: import { SystemState, UPDATE_SESSION, SystemActionTypes } from './types'
130: 
131: export function updateSession(newSession: SystemState): SystemActionTypes {
132:   return {
133:     type: UPDATE_SESSION,
134:     payload: newSession
135:   }
136: }
137: ```
138: 
139: ## Type Checking Reducers
140: 
141: Reducers are just pure functions that take the previous state, an action and then return the next state. In this example, we explicitly declare the type of actions this reducer will receive along with what it should return (the appropriate slice of state). With these additions TypeScript will give rich intellisense on the properties of our actions and state. In addition, we will also get errors when a certain case does not return the `ChatState`.
142: 
143: Type checked chat reducer:
144: 
145: ```ts
146: // src/store/chat/reducers.ts
147: 
148: import {
149:   ChatState,
150:   ChatActionTypes,
151:   SEND_MESSAGE,
152:   DELETE_MESSAGE
153: } from './types'
154: 
155: const initialState: ChatState = {
156:   messages: []
157: }
158: 
159: export function chatReducer(
160:   state = initialState,
161:   action: ChatActionTypes
162: ): ChatState {
163:   switch (action.type) {
164:     case SEND_MESSAGE:
165:       return {
166:         messages: [...state.messages, action.payload]
167:       }
168:     case DELETE_MESSAGE:
169:       return {
170:         messages: state.messages.filter(
171:           message => message.timestamp !== action.meta.timestamp
172:         )
173:       }
174:     default:
175:       return state
176:   }
177: }
178: ```

180: Type checked system reducer:
181: 
182: ```ts
183: // src/store/system/reducers.ts
184: 
185: import {
186:   SystemActions,
187:   SystemState,
188:   SystemActionTypes,
189:   UPDATE_SESSION
190: } from './types'
191: 
192: const initialState: SystemState = {
193:   loggedIn: false,
194:   session: '',
195:   userName: ''
196: }
197: 
198: export function systemReducer(
199:   state = initialState,
200:   action: SystemActionTypes
201: ): SystemState {
202:   switch (action.type) {
203:     case UPDATE_SESSION: {
204:       return {
205:         ...state,
206:         ...action.payload
207:       }
208:     }
209:     default:
210:       return state
211:   }
212: }
213: ```
214: 
215: We now need to generate the root reducer function, which is normally done using `combineReducers`. Note that we do not have to explicitly declare a new interface for AppState. We can use `ReturnType` to infer state shape from the `rootReducer`.
216: 
217: ```ts
218: // src/store/index.ts
219: 
220: import { systemReducer } from './system/reducers'
221: import { chatReducer } from './chat/reducers'
222: 
223: const rootReducer = combineReducers({
224:   system: systemReducer,
225:   chat: chatReducer
226: })
227: 
228: export type AppState = ReturnType<typeof rootReducer>
229: ```
230: 
231: ## Usage with React Redux
232: 
233: While React Redux is a separate library from redux itself, it is commonly used with react. For this reason, we will go through how React Redux works with TypeScript using the same example used previously in this section.
234: 
235: Note: React Redux does not have type checking by itself, you will have to install `@types/react-redux` by running `npm i @types/react-redux -D`.
236: 
237: We will now add type checking to the parameter that `mapStateToProps` receives. Luckily, we have already declared what the store should look like from defining a type that infers from the `rootReducer`:
238: 
239: ```ts
240: // src/App.tsx
241: 
242: import { AppState } from './store'
243: 
244: const mapStateToProps = (state: AppState) => ({
245:   system: state.system,
246:   chat: state.chat
247: })
248: ```
249: 
250: In this example we declared two different properties in `mapStateToProps`. To type check these properties, we will create an interface with the appropriate slices of state:
251: 
252: ```ts
253: // src/App.tsx
254: 
255: import { SystemState } from './store/system/types'
256: 
257: import { ChatState } from './store/chat/types'
258: 
259: interface AppProps {
260:   chat: ChatState
261:   system: SystemState
262: }
263: ```
264: 
265: We can now use this interface to specify what props the appropriate component will receive like so:
266: 
267: ```ts
268: // src/App.tsx
269: 
270: class App extends React.Component<AppProps> {
271: ```
272: 
273: In this component we are also mapping action creators to be available in the component's props. In the same `AppProps` interface we will use the powerful `typeof` feature to let TypeScript know what our action creators expect like so:
274: 
275: ```ts
276: // src/App.tsx
277: 
278: import { SystemState } from './store/system/types'
279: import { updateSession } from './store/system/actions'
280: 
281: import { ChatState } from './store/chat/types'
282: import { sendMessage } from './store/chat/actions'
283: 
284: interface AppProps {
285:   sendMessage: typeof sendMessage
286:   updateSession: typeof updateSession
287:   chat: ChatState
288:   system: SystemState
289: }
290: ```
291: 
292: With these additions made props that come from redux's side are now being type checked. Feel free to extend the interface as necessary to account for additional props being passed down from parent components.
293: 
294: ## Usage with Redux Thunk
295: 
296: Redux Thunk is a commonly used middleware for asynchronous orchestration. Feel free to check out its documentation [here](https://github.com/reduxjs/redux-thunk). A thunk is a function that returns another function that takes parameters `dispatch` and `getState`. Redux Thunk has a built in type `ThunkAction` which we can utilize like so:
297: 
298: ```ts
299: // src/thunks.ts
300: 
301: import { Action } from 'redux'
302: import { sendMessage } from './store/chat/actions'
303: import { AppState } from './store'
304: import { ThunkAction } from 'redux-thunk'
305: 
306: export const thunkSendMessage = (
307:   message: string
308: ): ThunkAction<void, AppState, null, Action<string>> => async dispatch => {
309:   const asyncResp = await exampleAPI()
310:   dispatch(
311:     sendMessage({
312:       message,
313:       user: asyncResp,
314:       timestamp: new Date().getTime()
315:     })
316:   )
317: }
318: 
319: function exampleAPI() {
320:   return Promise.resolve('Async Chat Bot')
321: }
322: ```
323: 
324: It is highly recommended to use action creators in your dispatch since we can reuse the work that has already been done to type check these functions.
325: 
326: ## Notes & Considerations
327: 
328: - This documentation covers primarily the redux side of type checking. For demonstration purposes, the codesandbox example also uses react with React Redux to demonstrate an integration.
329: - There are multiple approaches to type checking redux, this is just one of many approaches.
330: - This example only serves the purpose of showing this approach, meaning other advanced concepts have been stripped out to keep things simple. If you are code splitting your redux take a look at [this post](https://medium.com/@matthewgerstman/redux-with-code-splitting-and-type-checking-205195aded46).
331: - Understand that TypeScript does have its trade-offs. It is a good idea to understand when these trade-offs are worth it in your application.

First, we will install [React Testing Library](https://testing-library.com/react), which renders our components into a DOM and lets us interact with them the way a user would. It includes matchers for Jest through `@testing-library/jest-dom`:

```sh
npm install --save-dev @testing-library/react @testing-library/jest-dom
```

React Testing Library renders components into a DOM, which is provided by Jest's default `jsdom` test environment.

To test the components we make a `setup()` helper that passes the stubbed callbacks as props and renders the component with `render()`. This lets individual tests assert on whether the callbacks were called when expected by querying the rendered output and firing events the way a user would.

91: ## Installation
92: 
93: To install the stable version:
94: 
95: ```sh
96: npm install --save redux
97: ```
98: 
99: This assumes you are using [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/) as your package manager.
100: 
101: If you're not, you can [access these files on unpkg](https://unpkg.com/redux/), download them, or point your package manager to them.
102: 
103: Most commonly, people consume Redux as a collection of [CommonJS](https://github.com/webpack/docs/wiki/commonjs) modules. These modules are what you get when you import `redux` in a [Webpack](https://webpack.js.org/), [Browserify](http://browserify.org/), or a Node environment. If you like to live on the edge and use [Rollup](https://rollupjs.org), we support that as well.
104: 
105: If you don't use a module bundler, it's also fine. The `redux` npm package includes precompiled production and development [UMD](https://github.com/umdjs/umd) builds in the [`dist` folder](https://unpkg.com/redux/dist/). They can be used directly without a bundler and are thus compatible with many popular JavaScript module loaders and environments. For example, you can drop a UMD build as a [`<script>` tag](https://unpkg.com/redux/dist/redux.js) on the page, or [tell Bower to install it](https://github.com/reduxjs/redux/pull/1181#issuecomment-167361975). The UMD builds make Redux available as a `window.Redux` global variable.
106: 
107: The Redux source code is written in ES2015 but we precompile both CommonJS and UMD builds to ES5 so they work in [any modern browser](http://caniuse.com/#feat=es5). You don't need to use Babel or a module bundler to [get started with Redux](https://github.com/reduxjs/redux/blob/master/examples/counter-vanilla/index.html). You can even use the ES module build that's available at [`es/redux.mjs`](https://unpkg.com/redux/es/) which can be referenced using `type="module"` in your `script` tag or as a standard `import`.
108: 
109: ### Complementary Packages
110: 
111: Most likely, you'll also need [the React bindings](https://github.com/reduxjs/react-redux) and [the developer tools](https://github.com/reduxjs/redux-devtools).
112: 
113: ```sh
114: npm install --save react-redux
115: npm install --save-dev redux-devtools
116: ```
117: 
118: Note that unlike Redux itself, many packages in the Redux ecosystem don't provide UMD builds, so we recommend using CommonJS module bundlers like [Webpack](https://webpack.js.org/) and [Browserify](http://browserify.org/) for the most comfortable development experience.

7: 
8: # Installation
9: 
10: To install the stable version:
11: 
12: ```bash
13: npm install redux
14: ```
15: 
16: This assumes you are using [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/) as your package manager.
17: 
18: If you're not, you can [access these files on unpkg](https://unpkg.com/redux/), download them, or point your package manager to them.
19: 
20: Most commonly, people consume Redux as a collection of [CommonJS](http://webpack.github.io/docs/commonjs.html) modules. These modules are what you get when you import `redux` in a [Webpack](https://webpack.js.org/), [Browserify](http://browserify.org/), or a Node environment. If you like to live on the edge and use [Rollup](https://rollupjs.org), we support that as well.
21: 
22: If you don't use a module bundler, it's also fine. The `redux` npm package includes precompiled production and development [UMD](https://github.com/umdjs/umd) builds in the [`dist` folder](https://unpkg.com/redux/dist/). They can be used directly without a bundler and are thus compatible with many popular JavaScript module loaders and environments. For example, you can drop a UMD build as a [`<script>` tag](https://unpkg.com/redux/dist/redux.js) on the page, or [tell Bower to install it](https://github.com/reduxjs/redux/pull/1181#issuecomment-167361975). The UMD builds make Redux available as a `window.Redux` global variable.
23: 
24: The Redux source code is written in ES2015 but we precompile both CommonJS and UMD builds to ES5 so they work in [any modern browser](http://caniuse.com/#feat=es5). You don't need to use Babel or a module bundler to [get started with Redux](https://redux.js.org/introduction/examples#counter-vanilla).
25: 
26: ## Complementary Packages
27: 
28: Most likely, you'll also need [the React bindings](https://github.com/reduxjs/react-redux) and [the developer tools](https://github.com/reduxjs/redux-devtools).
29: 
30: ```bash
31: npm install react-redux
32: npm install --save-dev redux-devtools
33: ```
34: 
35: Note that unlike Redux itself, many packages in the Redux ecosystem don't provide UMD builds, so we recommend using CommonJS module bundlers like [Webpack](https://webpack.js.org/) and [Browserify](http://browserify.org/) for the most comfortable development experience.

(End of file - total 35 lines)
</content>

111: Redux notifies subscribers after each successfully dispatched action (i.e. an action reached the store and was handled by reducers). In some cases, it may be useful to cut down on the number of times subscribers are called, particularly if an action creator dispatches multiple distinct actions in a row.
112: 
113: There are several addons that add batching capabilities in various ways, like: [redux-batched-actions](https://github.com/tshelburne/redux-batched-actions) (a higher-order reducer that lets you dispatch several actions as if it was one and “unpack” them in the reducer), [redux-batched-subscribe](https://github.com/tappleby/redux-batched-subscribe) (a store enhancer that lets you debounce subscriber calls for multiple dispatches), or [redux-batch](https://github.com/manaflair/redux-batch) (a store enhancer that handles dispatching an array of actions with a single subscriber notification).
114: 
115: For React-Redux specifically, starting in [React-Redux v7](https://github.com/reduxjs/react-redux/releases/tag/v7.0.1) a new `batch` public API is available to help minimize the number of React re-renders when dispatching actions outside of React event handlers. It wraps React's `unstable_batchedUpdate()` API, allows any React updates in an event loop tick to be batched together into a single render pass. React already uses this internally for its own event handler callbacks. This API is actually part of the renderer packages like ReactDOM and React Native, not the React core itself.
116: 
117: Since React-Redux needs to work in both ReactDOM and React Native environments, we've taken care of importing this API from the correct renderer at build time for our own use. We also now re-export this function publicly ourselves, renamed to `batch()`. You can use it to ensure that multiple actions dispatched outside of React only result in a single render update, like this:
118: 
119: ```
120: import { batch } from "react-redux";
121: 
122: function myThunk() {
123:     return (dispatch, getState) => {
124:         // should only result in one combined re-render, not two
125:         batch(() => {
126:             dispatch(increment());
127:             dispatch(increment());
128:         })
129:     }
130: }
131: ```
132:

138: - [#542: Idea: batching actions](https://github.com/reduxjs/redux/issues/542)

8: # Usage with TypeScript
9: 
10: **TypeScript** is a typed superset of JavaScript. It has become popular recently in applications due to the benefits it can bring. If you are new to TypeScript it is highly recommended to become familiar with it first before proceeding. You can check out its documentation [here.](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/typescript-in-5-minutes.html)
11: 
12: TypeScript has the potential to bring the following benefits to a Redux application:
13: 
14: 1. Type safety for reducers, state and action creators
15: 2. Easy refactoring of typed code
16: 3. A superior developer experience in a team environment
17: 
18: ## A Practical Example
19: 
20: We will be going through a simplistic chat application to demonstrate a possible approach to include static typing. This chat application will have two reducers. The _chat reducer_ will focus on storing the chat history and the _system reducer_ will focus on storing session information.
21: 
22: The full source code is available on [codesandbox here](https://codesandbox.io/s/w02m7jm3q7). Note that by going through this example yourself you will experience some of the benefits of using TypeScript.
23: 
24: ## Type Checking State
25: 
26: Adding types to each slice of state is a good place to start since it does not rely on other types. In this example we start by describing the chat reducer's slice of state:
27: 
28: ```ts
29: // src/store/chat/types.ts
30: 
31: export interface Message {
32:   user: string
33:   message: string
34:   timestamp: number
35: }
36: 
37: export interface ChatState {
38:   messages: Message[]
39: }
40: ```
41: 
42: And then do the same for the system reducer's slice of state:
43: 
44: ```ts
45: // src/store/system/types.ts
46: 
47: export interface SystemState {
48:   loggedIn: boolean
49:   session: string
50:   userName: string
51: }
52: ```
53: 
54: Note that we are exporting these interfaces to reuse them later in reducers and action creators.
55: 
56: ## Type Checking Actions & Action Creators
57: 
58: We will be using string literals and using `typeof` to declare our action constants and infer types. Note that we are making a tradeoff here when we declare our types in a separate file. In exchange for separating our types into a separate file, we get to keep our other files more focused on their purpose. While this tradeoff can improve the maintainability of the codebase, it is perfectly fine to organize your project however you see fit.
59: 
60: Chat Action Constants & Shape:
61: 
62: ```ts
63: // src/store/chat/types.ts
64: export const SEND_MESSAGE = 'SEND_MESSAGE'
65: export const DELETE_MESSAGE = 'DELETE_MESSAGE'
66: 
67: interface SendMessageAction {
68:   type: typeof SEND_MESSAGE
69:   payload: Message
70: }
71: 
72: interface DeleteMessageAction {
73:   type: typeof DELETE_MESSAGE
74:   meta: {
75:     timestamp: number
76:   }
77: }
78: 
79: export type ChatActionTypes = SendMessageAction | DeleteMessageAction
80: ```

139: ## Type Checking Reducers
140: 
141: Reducers are just pure functions that take the previous state, an action and then return the next state. In this example, we explicitly declare the type of actions this reducer will receive along with what it should return (the appropriate slice of state). With these additions TypeScript will give rich intellisense on the properties of our actions and state. In addition, we will also get errors when a certain case does not return the `ChatState`.
142: 
143: Type checked chat reducer:
144: 
145: ```ts
146: // src/store/chat/reducers.ts
147: 
148: import {
149:   ChatState,
150:   ChatActionTypes,
151:   SEND_MESSAGE,
152:   DELETE_MESSAGE
153: } from './types'
154: 
155: const initialState: ChatState = {
156:   messages: []
157: }
158: 
159: export function chatReducer(
160:   state = initialState,
161:   action: ChatActionTypes
162: ): ChatState {
163:   switch (action.type) {
164:     case SEND_MESSAGE:
165:       return {
166:         messages: [...state.messages, action.payload]
167:       }
168:     case DELETE_MESSAGE:
169:       return {
170:         messages: state.messages.filter(
171:           message => message.timestamp !== action.meta.timestamp
172:         )
173:       }
174:     default:
175:       return state
176:   }
177: }
178: ```
179: 
180: Type checked system reducer:
181: 
182: ```ts
183: // src/store/system/reducers.ts
184: 
185: import {
186:   SystemActions,
187:   SystemState,
188:   SystemActionTypes,
189:   UPDATE_SESSION
190: } from './types'
191: 
192: const initialState: SystemState = {
193:   loggedIn: false,
194:   session: '',
195:   userName: ''
196: }
197: 
198: export function systemReducer(
199:   state = initialState,
200:   action: SystemActionTypes
201: ): SystemState {
202:   switch (action.type) {
203:     case UPDATE_SESSION: {
204:       return {
205:         ...state,
206:         ...action.payload
207:       }
208:     }
209:     default:
210:       return state
211:   }
212: }
213: ```
214: 
215: We now need to generate the root reducer function, which is normally done using `combineReducers`. Note that we do not have to explicitly declare a new interface for AppState. We can use `ReturnType` to infer state shape from the `rootReducer`.
216: 
217: ```ts
218: // src/store/index.ts
219: 
220: import { systemReducer } from './system/reducers'
221: import { chatReducer } from './chat/reducers'
222: 
223: const rootReducer = combineReducers({
224:   system: systemReducer,
225:   chat: chatReducer
226: })
227: 
228: export type AppState = ReturnType<typeof rootReducer>
229: ```

231: ## Usage with React Redux
232: 
233: While React Redux is a separate library from redux itself, it is commonly used with react. For this reason, we will go through how React Redux works with TypeScript using the same example used previously in this section.
234: 
235: Note: React Redux does not have type checking by itself, you will have to install `@types/react-redux` by running `npm i @types/react-redux -D`.
236: 
237: We will now add type checking to the parameter that `mapStateToProps` receives. Luckily, we have already declared what the store should look like from defining a type that infers from the `rootReducer`:
238: 
239: ```ts
240: // src/App.tsx
241: 
242: import { AppState } from './store'
243: 
244: const mapStateToProps = (state: AppState) => ({
245:   system: state.system,
246:   chat: state.chat
247: })
248: ```
249: 
250: In this example we declared two different properties in `mapStateToProps`. To type check these properties, we will create an interface with the appropriate slices of state:
251: 
252: ```ts
253: // src/App.tsx
254: 
255: import { SystemState } from './store/system/types'
256: 
257: import { ChatState } from './store/chat/types'
258: 
259: interface AppProps {
260:   chat: ChatState
261:   system: SystemState
262: }
263: ```
264: 
265: We can now use this interface to specify what props the appropriate component will receive like so:
266: 
267: ```ts
268: // src/App.tsx
269: 
270: class App extends React.Component<AppProps> {
271: ```
272: 
273: In this component we are also mapping action creators to be available in the component's props. In the same `AppProps` interface we will use the powerful `typeof` feature to let TypeScript know what our action creators expect like so:
274: 
275: ```ts
276: // src/App.tsx
277: 
278: import { SystemState } from './store/system/types'
279: import { updateSession } from './store/system/actions'
280: 
281: import { ChatState } from './store/chat/types'
282: import { sendMessage } from './store/chat/actions'
283: 
284: interface AppProps {
285:   sendMessage: typeof sendMessage
286:   updateSession: typeof updateSession
287:   chat: ChatState
288:   system: SystemState
289: }
290: ```
291: 
292: With these additions made props that come from redux's side are now being type checked. Feel free to extend the interface as necessary to account for additional props being passed down from parent components.
293: 
294: ## Usage with Redux Thunk
295: 
296: Redux Thunk is a commonly used middleware for asynchronous orchestration. Feel free to check out its documentation [here](https://github.com/reduxjs/redux-thunk). A thunk is a function that returns another function that takes parameters `dispatch` and `getState`. Redux Thunk has a built in type `ThunkAction` which we can utilize like so:
297: 
298: ```ts
299: // src/thunks.ts
300: 
301: import { Action } from 'redux'
302: import { sendMessage } from './store/chat/actions'
303: import { AppState } from './store'
304: import { ThunkAction } from 'redux-thunk'
305: 
306: export const thunkSendMessage = (
307:   message: string
308: ): ThunkAction<void, AppState, unknown, Action<string>> => async dispatch => {
309:   const asyncResp = await exampleAPI()
310:   dispatch(
311:     sendMessage({
312:       message,
313:       user: asyncResp,
314:       timestamp: new Date().getTime()
315:     })
316:   )
317: }
318: 
319: function exampleAPI() {
320:   return Promise.resolve('Async Chat Bot')
321: }
322: ```
323: 
324: It is highly recommended to use action creators in your dispatch since we can reuse the work that has already been done to type check these functions.
325: 
326: ## Notes & Considerations
327: 
328: - This documentation covers primarily the redux side of type checking. For demonstration purposes, the codesandbox example also uses react with React Redux to demonstrate an integration.
329: - There are multiple approaches to type checking redux, this is just one of many approaches.
330: - This example only serves the purpose of showing this approach, meaning other advanced concepts have been stripped out to keep things simple. If you are code splitting your redux take a look at [this post](https://medium.com/@matthewgerstman/redux-with-code-splitting-and-type-checking-205195aded46).
331: - Understand that TypeScript does have its trade-offs. It is a good idea to understand when these trade-offs are worth it in your application.
